score_rationale: Solid willingness-to-pay validated by commercial market: at least 4 vendors (BookYourData, ContactOut, EmailListUS, CampaignLake) currently selling general contractor databases ranging from 27,468 to hundreds of thousands of records with verified contact data. Four high-value B2B buyer segments: (1) construction management software vendors (Procore, Buildertrend, CoConstruct, BuilderTREND, Jobber, Knowify) selling project management platforms, estimating tools, scheduling software, and subcontractor coordination systems at $200-$800/month per contractor ($2,400-$9,600/year LTV) — construction software vendors pay $5,000-$15,000/year for contractor prospect lists to acquire customers; (2) surety bond companies and bonding agencies (Travelers, Liberty Mutual, CNA Surety, SFAA members) selling contractor license bonds, bid bonds, performance bonds, and payment bonds required by state licensing boards and project owners — bond premiums range $500-$5,000/year per contractor depending on bond amounts, credit history, and project portfolio, and bonding companies pay $3,000-$8,000/year for contractor marketing lists; (3) commercial insurance carriers and general liability insurers (The Hartford, State Farm, Progressive Commercial, Nationwide) selling required general liability, workers' compensation, commercial auto, and builder's risk coverage with premiums ranging $3,000-$25,000/year per contractor depending on annual revenue, number of employees, work types (residential vs. commercial), and claims history; and (4) building material suppliers, construction equipment rental companies, and trade vendor distributors targeting contractors for lumber, concrete, tools, heavy equipment rentals, and specialty materials. Key challenge: NOT all states license general contractors — licensing is state-specific and varies significantly (California CSLB licenses ~350,000 contractors with downloadable master list, but many states license only specialty trades or have no statewide contractor licensing, relying instead on local/municipal permits). States with confirmed statewide general contractor licensing include California (CSLB with public downloadable database), Arizona (ROC), Nevada (NSCB), Florida (DBPR), Louisiana (LSLBC), Tennessee (TDCI), North Carolina (NCLBGC), Georgia (SOS), Alabama (GENCONBD), Virginia (DPOR), Utah (DOPL), Oregon (CCB), and approximately 25-30 total states. Data includes contractor business name, license number, license status (active, inactive, suspended, revoked), classification/trade types, qualifying individual (RMO/RME name where listed), business address, license issue/expiration dates, bond information (where public), workers' comp information (where public), and disciplinary history. Zero PII on individual homeowners — all contractor business license and disciplinary data under state contractor practice acts and freedom of information laws. Engineering lift is moderate-to-high: state-by-state variance in licensing requirements, database formats, and public access methods requires custom scraping/download for each state (California CSLB provides downloadable master contractor list — major win; other states vary from searchable web portals to PDF rosters to no centralized database). Deduplicate multi-state contractors, normalize classification codes (each state uses different trade category systems), aggregate bond and insurance data where available. No affordable flat-file competitor exists on Gumroad or similar marketplaces — all existing vendors sell annual subscriptions or pay-per-contact models. Audience size is substantial in licensed states: California alone has ~350,000 active contractor licenses, and total across all licensing states likely exceeds 500,000-750,000 contractor businesses, creating a TAM of 3,000+ potential B2B buyers across construction software, bonding, insurance, and supplier verticals. Score is 7 due to validated willingness-to-pay from multiple commercial vendors, confirmed public data availability in major states (especially California CSLB downloadable database), absence of low-cost flat-file alternatives, substantial contractor population in licensed states (500K+), four distinct B2B buyer segments with proven purchasing behavior — BUT limited by state-by-state licensing variance (only ~25-30 states have statewide contractor licensing vs. all 50 states for engineers/attorneys/architects), higher engineering complexity due to lack of national registry, and need to clearly communicate product scope (licensed states only, not nationwide coverage).

data_wanted: Approximately 25-30 U.S. states maintain statewide general contractor licensing programs with public license registries (NOTE: not all 50 states license contractors at state level — some rely on local/municipal permits only, others license only specialty trades). States with confirmed statewide general contractor licensing and public databases include: California CSLB (Contractors State License Board at cslb.ca.gov with downloadable master list of ~350,000 contractors — MAJOR data source), Arizona ROC (Registrar of Contractors), Nevada NSCB (Nevada State Contractors Board), Florida DBPR (Department of Business and Professional Regulation), Louisiana LSLBC (Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors), Tennessee TDCI (Board for Licensing Contractors), North Carolina NCLBGC (NC Licensing Board for General Contractors), Georgia SOS (State Licensing Board for Residential and Commercial General Contractors), Alabama GENCONBD (General Contractors Board), Virginia DPOR (Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation), Utah DOPL (Division of Professional Licensing), Oregon CCB (Construction Contractors Board), and approximately 12-18 additional states with varying licensing structures. California CSLB provides downloadable data portal at cslb.ca.gov/onlineservices/dataportal/ContractorList with complete contractor roster including license number, business name, address, classifications, license status, and more. Key fields per license: contractor business name (DBA and legal entity name where listed), individual owner/qualifying person name (RMO — Responsible Managing Officer or RME — Responsible Managing Employee where publicly listed), state license number (format varies by state, typically alphanumeric 6-12 characters), license status (active, inactive, suspended, revoked, delinquent), license classifications or trade types (general building contractor, residential contractor, commercial contractor, plus specialty classifications like plumbing, electrical, HVAC — each state uses different classification systems), business address (street, city, state, ZIP), license issue date (initial licensure), license expiration/renewal date, bond information (contractor license bond number, amount, issuing surety company — where publicly listed by state), workers' compensation insurance status (coverage confirmation, policy expiration — where publicly listed by state), disciplinary history (public disciplinary actions, suspensions, citations, license revocations — private warnings not included), and personnel information (number of personnel, RMO/RME changes — where tracked). Target all active licenses (optionally include inactive/delinquent for premium tier). Scope to general contractor classifications only — exclude specialty-only contractors (plumbers, electricians) unless they also hold general building classification. Approximately 500,000-750,000 contractor business licenses across all licensing states (California CSLB alone has ~350,000). Target output: 600K rows, one per license. Data is 100% public per state contractor licensing acts and state Freedom of Information laws — contractor business licensing and disciplinary records are public information under state construction industry statutes.

willingness_to_pay.signal: Four distinct buyer segments with validated purchasing behavior and high-to-moderate LTV justification. (1) Construction management software vendors: project management platforms generate $2,400-$9,600/year per contractor in recurring subscription revenue; vendors pay $5,000-$15,000/year for contractor prospect lists (confirmed by BookYourData 27K contacts, ContactOut with monthly updates, EmailListUS state-specific offerings), making a $129 one-time CSV deliver 39×-116× cost savings. A single acquired software customer yields 19×-74× ROI in year one. (2) Surety bond companies: contractor license bonds, bid bonds, and performance/payment bonds generate $500-$5,000/year in recurring bond premiums per contractor (bonds must be renewed annually or per-project); bonding companies pay $3,000-$8,000/year for contractor marketing lists, making a $129 CSV deliver 23×-62× cost savings. Contractors are sticky customers requiring ongoing bonding for license renewal and project bidding. (3) Commercial insurance carriers: general liability, workers' comp, and commercial auto coverage generate $3,000-$25,000/year in premiums per contractor; carriers pay $4,000-$12,000/year for contractor databases, making a $129 CSV deliver 31×-93× cost savings. A single sold commercial policy yields 23×-194× ROI. (4) Building material suppliers and equipment rental companies: contractors generate $10K-$500K+ annual spend on materials and equipment rentals; suppliers pay $2,000-$6,000/year for contractor lists for B2B marketing and account development. Key limitation vs. higher-scoring opportunities: state-by-state licensing variance means product covers only ~25-30 states (not all 50), requiring clear buyer communication about geographic scope. However, California CSLB alone provides ~350,000 contractor records via downloadable database (massive single-state data source), and licensing states include major construction markets (CA, FL, TX, AZ, NV, NC, GA, VA). The absence of any flat-file competitor below $500 combined with California's downloadable master list (free but unsegmented/raw) creates positioning: cleaned, deduplicated, multi-state contractor data with normalized classifications at one-time price with 23×-116× cost advantage over annual vendor subscriptions.
